day_title: Twelve Years And Everything She Had
reflection_question: How long has this been going on, and what have you already tried? Write the list without judging yourself for it.
devotional_text:
Some of you have been fighting this a very long time.

Long enough that hope has become something you are suspicious of. You have been encouraged before. You have started before. You have been to the thing, read the book, made the promise, had the good month.

This day is for you.

# Twelve Years

> "A certain woman, who had an issue of blood for twelve years, and had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse." (Mark 5:25-26)

Read that slowly, because there are four separate griefs in it.

* ⏳ **Twelve years.** Not a bad season. Over a decade.
* 🏥 **Suffered many things by many physicians.** She tried. Repeatedly. The treatments themselves hurt.
* 💸 **Spent all that she had.** It took her money as well as her health.
* 📉 **Was no better, but rather grew worse.** Everything she tried left her worse than before.

If you have ever thought *I have already tried everything and it only got worse*, somebody wrote your sentence down two thousand years ago.

## And There Is A Fifth Thing

Under Jewish law, her condition made her ceremonially unclean. Continuously. For twelve years.

That meant no temple. It meant anyone who touched her became unclean too.

So she had not been properly touched, or fully included, in twelve years.

The illness was one problem. **The isolation was the other one, and it probably hurt more.**

## What She Does

> "Having heard the things concerning Jesus, came up behind him in the crowd, and touched his clothes." (Mark 5:27)

From behind.

She does not ask. She does not come round the front and explain her situation to a rabbi in public, because she knows exactly how that conversation would go.

She comes from behind and takes hold of the edge of His coat and hopes nobody notices.

That is not weak faith. That is the faith of somebody who has been humiliated enough times to be careful. It still counted.

> "For she said, 'If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well.'" (Mark 5:28)

## He Stops The Whole Thing

Here is the part that matters.

Jesus is on His way somewhere urgent — a man's daughter is dying — and He stops.

> "Who touched my clothes?" (Mark 5:30)

The disciples think He is being ridiculous. There are hundreds of people pressed in around Him.

But He keeps looking.

Why? She had already been healed. He could have let her slip away with what she came for.

**Because being healed in secret would have left the other half of it untreated.**

She would have gone home well and still hidden. Still the woman who took something she was not supposed to have. Still unclean in her own mind.

He stops a crowd, in the middle of an emergency, to deal with her shame and not just her illness.

## What She Does Then

> "But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had been done to her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth." (Mark 5:33)

**Told him all the truth.** In front of everybody. Twelve years of it.

Fearing and trembling. It cost her enormously.

And what comes back is one word that changes her whole standing.

> "Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease." (Mark 5:34)

**Daughter.**

It is the only time in the gospels Jesus calls a woman that.

Twelve years of untouchable, and the first word He gives her is a family word.

## What To Watch For In Mark 5:21-34

* 🔢 The four things verse 26 says about what she had already been through
* 🧥 How she approaches, in verse 27 — from behind, without asking
* ⏸️ That Jesus stops on the way to a dying child
* 🔍 "He looked around to see her" in verse 32 — He keeps looking
* 🗣️ That she tells the whole truth publicly, and what He calls her afterwards

## The Bigger Takeaway

The length of this does not disqualify you.

Twelve years of failed attempts did not make her a lost cause. It made her the one He stopped a crowd for.

And notice: **she was not healed because she had finally found the right technique.** She had tried every technique in the country. She was healed because she got to Him, badly, from behind, in a crowd, with no dignity left.

That is available to you this morning.

## Today's One Thing

**Write the list of everything you have already tried.**

Every attempt. The programmes, the promises, the apps, the accountability that fizzled, the geographic moves, the relationships you hoped would fix it.

Write them all down, and here is the instruction that matters: **do not sneer at a single one of them.**

That list is not evidence that you are hopeless. It is evidence that you have been fighting for years, and nobody who had given up would have a list that long.

Then, at the bottom, write: *and I am still here, and I am still asking.*

## Today's Prayer

Jesus,

I have been at this a long time.

I have tried things that did not work and some that made it worse, and I have spent money and years and people on it.

I am past the point of coming to You confidently. I am coming the way she did — from behind, in the crowd, hoping.

Stop for me.

And if there is a part of this that needs to come out into the open before it can really be dealt with, give me what she had, because she was frightened and she said it all anyway.

I would like to hear You call me something other than what I have been calling myself.

In Your name, amen.

reflection_question: What do you assume God thinks of you after your worst failure? Where did that assumption actually come from?
devotional_text:
Peter denied he even knew Jesus. Three times. Out loud. To strangers. While Jesus was being tried a short distance away.

And the last one, Luke tells us, happened just as Jesus turned and looked at him.

Then Jesus died, and Peter had to live with that as the last thing between them.

If you have ever thought *there is no coming back from what I did*, Peter is your man.

# He Goes Back To Fishing

After the resurrection, Peter has seen Jesus alive. And then he says this:

*I am going fishing.*

Back to the boats. Back to what he was doing before any of it started.

That is what shame does. It sends you backwards. Not to sin necessarily — to smallness. To the version of your life from before you believed anything good about yourself.

You know this move. After a bad stretch you quietly stop reaching for things. You stop praying out loud. You stop putting yourself forward. You go back to the boats.

## Jesus Shows Up On The Shore

They catch nothing all night. A man on the beach tells them to throw the net on the other side, and it comes up full, and John says *it is the Lord*.

Peter throws himself into the water and swims.

That is worth noticing. He is ashamed, and he still swims toward Him. Both things at once.

## And There Is A Fire

> "So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid on it, and bread." (John 21:9)

A charcoal fire.

There is only one other charcoal fire in John's gospel. It is the one Peter was standing at, warming his hands, when he said *I do not know the man*.

Jesus built the same fire.

Not to punish him. To take him back to the exact place it happened, and do it differently.

**He does not avoid the scene of the failure. He returns to it with breakfast.**

## Three Questions

> "Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?" (John 21:15)

Three denials. Three questions.

And Peter is hurt by the third one — the text says *grieved* — because he can count, and he knows exactly what is being undone.

> "Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you." (John 21:17)

He stops defending himself. He appeals to the fact that Jesus already knows.

That is where you landed on Day 10, and it is the only honest ground any of us have.

## What Jesus Does With Him

After each answer, a job.

*Feed my lambs. Tend my sheep. Feed my sheep.*

Not *sit down for a few years and prove yourself*.

**Work. Immediately. Responsibility for other people.**

This is the man who failed most publicly in the entire New Testament, and within a few weeks he is preaching the sermon where three thousand people come to faith.

## What This Is Not

It is not a promise that there are no consequences. Peter carried that memory for life.

It is a promise about *standing*. Peter's place with Jesus was not downgraded. He did not become a second-tier disciple with an asterisk next to his name.

He was restored to the same ground he was on before, and then given more to do.

## What To Watch For In John 21:1-19

* 🎣 What Peter decides to do in verse 3, after everything
* 🏊 That he swims toward Jesus while still carrying what he did
* 🔥 The charcoal fire in verse 9, and where the only other one in John is
* 3️⃣ The number of questions, and why Peter is grieved by the third
* 🐑 What follows each answer — a task, not a probation

## The Bigger Takeaway

You have decided what God thinks of you after your worst night.

You did not get that verdict from Him. You assembled it from somewhere else and have been serving the sentence ever since.

Jesus walked Peter back to the fire, cooked him breakfast, asked him three times, and put him to work.

**That is what restoration looks like. It is specific, it goes back to the exact place it happened, and it ends with being trusted again.**

## Today's One Thing

**Name your charcoal fire.**

The specific scene. The night, the room, the conversation, the thing you said or did that you have decided is the end of the story.

Write it down in one sentence.

Then, underneath, write what Jesus asked Peter, with your own name in it:

*______, do you love me?*

And answer it. Honestly, in whatever broken form it comes out.

That is the question He asks after the worst thing. Not *how could you*. Just: *do you still want me?*

## Today's Prayer

Jesus,

I have a night I cannot get past.

I have treated it as the end of what You and I could be. I have been going back to the boats ever since, keeping my head down, not expecting much.

You built the same fire for Peter. You took him back to the exact spot and You fed him there.

Do that with me.

Ask me the question. I will answer it badly, the way he did, but I will answer it.

And then give me something to do, because I have spent long enough believing I am only fit to sit at the back.

In Your name, amen.

day_title: He Knows What It Feels Like
reflection_question: When you pray about this, what tone do you use? What would change if you came 'with boldness' instead?
devotional_text:
There is a particular loneliness in being told to take something to God by people who have obviously never felt what you feel.

It makes God sound like a very clean person being told about a very dirty problem.

Hebrews 4 says something that cuts straight through that.

# The Sentence

> "For we don't have a high priest who can't be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin." (Hebrews 4:15)

Unpack it, because the double negative hides how strong it is.

We do **not** have a high priest who **cannot** be touched with the feeling of our weaknesses.

In plain English: **the one you are praying to can feel what this feels like.**

Not in theory. Not from a distance. Not as an expert who has read about it.

## "In All Points Tempted Like We Are"

That phrase is doing a lot of work.

In all points. Not in some tidy, abstract, religious way. The whole range.

And then four words that people often read as the end of the sentence when actually they deepen it: **yet without sin.**

Here is what most people miss about that.

If you give in to temptation at twenty minutes, you only ever experience twenty minutes of its pressure. The person who never gives in is the one who feels the *full* weight of it, all the way to the end.

So "without sin" does not mean He had it easier. It means He felt more of it than you ever have.

**He is not a God who does not understand. He is the only one who has felt the whole thing.**

## Why This Changes How You Pray

Look at what the writer concludes from it.

> "Let us therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy, and may find grace for help in time of need." (Hebrews 4:16)

**Boldness.**

Not creeping in. Not apologising for existing. Not the small, flat, defeated voice you have been using.

Think about how you actually pray about this. Most people in this fight pray like somebody handing in a late assignment for the ninth time. *Sorry. I know. It is me again.*

Hebrews says come boldly, and the reason you can is not that you are doing well. It is that the one on the throne knows exactly how hard it is from the inside.

## "Grace For Help In Time Of Need"

That phrase is practical, not poetic.

*In time of need* means **at the moment it is happening.** Not afterwards, in the confession. During.

Which means you can pray at the worst possible second. Mid-craving. Hand already reaching. Browser already open.

A lot of people believe prayer is only available to them when they are behaving. So in the actual moment of temptation, the one place they never go is to God — because it feels dishonest to ask for help with something you are three seconds from choosing.

It is not dishonest. It is the entire point of the verse.

## The Verse Before It

And just before all this, there is a line that makes it honest rather than sentimental:

> "The word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword... and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart." (Hebrews 4:12)

That is the same passage. God sees straight through you, **and** He is touched with the feeling of your weakness.

Both. Together. That combination is the only one that actually helps — a God who cannot be fooled and does not condemn you.

## What To Watch For In Hebrews 4:12-16

* 🗡️ What the word of God is compared to in verse 12
* 👁️ "All things are naked and laid open" in verse 13 — nothing hidden
* 🤝 The double negative in verse 15, and what it is actually saying
* ⛰️ "In all points" — the range of it
* 🏃 The instruction in verse 16, and the word "boldness"
* ⏱️ "In time of need" — when the grace is for

## The Bigger Takeaway

You have been praying as though you are explaining your problem to somebody who could not possibly relate.

You are not. You are talking to the one person who has felt the absolute limit of that pressure and did not break.

**He is not embarrassed by this conversation. He is the only one qualified to have it.**

## Today's One Thing

**Pray once in the moment.**

Today, or the next time it rises — not after, not tomorrow in your quiet time — say one sentence to God while it is happening.

It does not have to be good. It can be one word. *Help.*

It can be honest to the point of rude: *I want this and I do not want to want it.*

The point is to break the habit of going silent at exactly the moment you most need to speak.

You have been treating the craving as a private room God is not allowed into. Let Him in, mid-sentence, before you have sorted yourself out.

**That is what "grace for help in time of need" means. Use it at the time of need.**

## Today's Prayer

Jesus,

I have been praying to You like a man handing in the same apology over and over.

Small voice. Head down. Expecting nothing much.

Your word says You know what this feels like. Not as information. As experience. That You felt the full weight of it and did not fold, which means You know more about it than I do, not less.

So I am going to stop creeping.

Help me in the moment. Not afterwards, when it is a confession. Help me at 11 p.m. with my hand already moving.

I am coming boldly, because You said I could, and because today I have nothing else to come with.

In Your name, amen.

reflection_question: What do you secretly believe could make God give up on you? Hold that specific thing up against Romans 8:38-39.
devotional_text:
This is the last day before we start turning.

For eight days we have looked at who God is when He finds you — in the desert, in the circle of accusers, under the broom tree, at the charcoal fire.

Today we settle the question underneath all of it.

**Can I lose Him by doing this again?**

Because if the answer is yes, everything in the next forty days is built on sand. You will be trying to change in order to keep Him, which is the most exhausting and least effective reason to change there is.

# Paul Asks It As Questions

Romans 8 ends with a series of questions, and each one is aimed at a specific fear.

> "If God is for us, who can be against us?" (Romans 8:31)

> "Who could bring a charge against God's chosen ones? It is God who justifies." (Romans 8:33)

Stop there a second.

Who brings the charge against you? Every morning after?

Usually it is you. Sometimes it is a person. Sometimes it is something older and darker than either.

Paul's answer is not *the charge is false*. He does not pretend you did nothing.

His answer is: **the judge has already ruled.** It is God who justifies. The case is closed and the verdict was given before you woke up this morning.

## And Then The One That Matters

> "Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us." (Romans 8:34)

Read the last part again.

**Who also makes intercession for us.**

Right now. While you are reading this. Whatever you did last night.

The one person with the standing to condemn you is instead speaking on your behalf.

## The List

Then Paul starts listing everything he can think of that might separate you from God's love, and he does not pick gentle examples.

> "Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" (Romans 8:35)

And then the big one:

> "For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from God's love, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." (Romans 8:38-39)

He is deliberately trying to leave nothing out.

Death. Life. The present. The future. Powers. Height. Depth.

And then, in case he has missed something: **"nor any other created thing."**

That phrase is there for you.

Because you have an exception in mind. Everybody in this fight does. *Yes, but not this. Not what I did. Not after this many times.*

Paul closed that door on purpose. Whatever your exception is, it is a created thing, and it is on the list.

## What This Does Not Mean

Be careful, because there is a lazy version of this.

The lazy version says: nothing can separate me, so it does not matter what I do.

Paul deals with that directly two chapters earlier — *shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? May it never be!* We will spend Day 47 on exactly that question.

Security is not permission. **It is the ground you stand on while you fight, instead of the prize you are fighting for.**

There is a world of difference between a child who might be thrown out and a child who knows they will not. One of them hides everything. The other can afford to tell the truth.

## What To Watch For In Romans 8:31-39

* ❓ How many of these verses are questions rather than statements
* ⚖️ Who the judge is, in verse 33
* 🙏 What Christ is doing right now, at the end of verse 34
* 📋 The length of the list in verses 38 and 39, and how hard Paul works to be exhaustive
* 🚪 The phrase "nor any other created thing"

## The Bigger Takeaway

You have been fighting this while half believing that each failure moves you further from God, and that one day you will go too far.

If that were true, every relapse would be a step toward being abandoned — and the fear of that is itself one of the things that drives people back to the thing.

**Paul says the floor does not move.**

And that changes what the next forty days are. You are not trying to earn your way back into His affection.

You are already in it, and now you are learning to live like somebody who is.

## Today's One Thing

**Write your exception, and then answer it.**

On one line, write the thing you secretly believe could finally make God give up on you. Be specific. The real one.

Under it, copy out Romans 8:38-39 in full, by hand.

Then draw a line through your exception.

Not because it did not happen. Because it is a created thing, and Paul already put it on the list.

Keep that piece of paper. There will be a morning in the next forty days when you need it.

## Today's Prayer

God,

I have been carrying a quiet fear that one day I will do it once too often and You will be finished with me.

I have never said it out loud because it sounds like bad theology. But it is what I have actually believed, and it has shaped the way I have prayed for years.

Your word says nothing can separate me. Not the future. Not powers. Not any created thing.

I want to believe that in the hour it matters, not just in a quiet room on a Friday morning.

So settle it in me.

Not so I can take advantage of it. So I can stop fighting You and start fighting this.

In Jesus' name, amen.

day_title: He Is Not Finished With You
reflection_question: Look back at Day 1. What is different about how you are thinking now, even if nothing is different about your behaviour yet?
devotional_text:
Twenty days.

You have named it, looked at the lie, felt the weight of the secret, found the thirst underneath, understood why trying harder fails, counted the cost, seen it from outside, survived a morning after, found out you are not alone, handed over the last part.

And then eight days of who God is when He finds you.

Some of you have not used in those twenty days. Some of you have, more than once.

**Both of you are still here, and that matters more than you think.**

# One Verse

> "Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ." (Philippians 1:6)

Three things in it.

## "He Who Began"

Not you.

Something started before you decided anything. The fact that you opened this study at all, that something in you was still restless about this, that you have not simply made peace with it — that was not generated by your own willpower.

You did not begin this. You responded to it.

## "A Good Work In You"

In you. Present tense. Now.

Not *will begin if you get your act together*.

Whatever your last twenty days have actually looked like, there is work going on, and it is being described as good.

That is hard to accept on a day when nothing visible has changed. But most of what has happened in these twenty days has been invisible by design — honesty, naming, seeing clearly. None of that shows up in behaviour yet.

**Foundations do not look like progress. They look like a hole in the ground.**

## "Will Complete It"

This is the part to hold.

God does not abandon projects.

The timeline is longer than you want — "until the day of Jesus Christ" is a lifetime, not a quarter — and that is deliberately said, because the thing that breaks most people is expecting it to be finished by March.

But the direction is settled. He finishes what He starts.

## Who Paul Wrote This To

He wrote it from prison. To a church he loved, that had its own mess — he spends part of the letter telling two women to sort out an argument.

So it is not a verse from somebody for whom everything was going well, written to people who had it together.

It is a chained man writing to a flawed church: *He will finish it.*

## What The Next Forty Days Are

Tomorrow the study turns.

The first twenty days were about telling the truth and meeting the God who already knew it. That had to come first, because every attempt that skips it collapses — you cannot repent of something you have not admitted, and you will not run toward a God you are frightened of.

From tomorrow:

* 🔄 **Days 21-30.** Turning. What repentance actually is, and why it is not the same as feeling bad.
* 🧱 **Days 31-40.** Rebuilding. Triggers, hours, habits, your body, the people near you.
* 🩹 **Days 41-50.** When you fall. Because some of you will, and what you do next decides everything.
* 🌅 **Days 51-60.** A life bigger than this.

It gets more practical from here. But none of the practical parts work without the twenty days you have just done.

## What To Watch For In Philippians 1:1-11

* 🙏 How Paul describes praying for them in verses 3 and 4 — with joy
* 🤝 "Your partnership in furtherance of the Good News" in verse 5
* 🏗️ Who began the work, who completes it, and how long it takes
* ❤️ What he actually prays for them in verse 9 — love abounding in knowledge and discernment
* ⛓️ That he is in prison while writing all of this

## The Bigger Takeaway

If you have used in the last twenty days, you may be reading this feeling like a fraud.

You are not twenty days of progress. You are twenty days of honesty, and honesty is the only ground that progress has ever grown in.

**He who began a good work in you will complete it.**

Not *might*. Not *if you manage the next part well*.

Will.

## Today's One Thing

**Go back and read Day 1.**

Read what you wrote. Read the sentence you said out loud twenty days ago.

Then write one paragraph: what is different in how you *think* about this now, even if nothing is different in what you have *done*?

Maybe you have stopped calling it a bad habit. Maybe you have told one person. Maybe you have noticed the argument in your head and recognised it for the first time. Maybe you simply have not given up, which twenty days ago you were close to doing.

Write it down. You will want it on Day 45.

## Today's Prayer

God,

Twenty days.

Some of them went well. Some of them did not, and You know exactly which.

I expected to feel further along than this. Part of me wants to call the whole thing a failure already, because that is what I do.

But Your word says You started something in me, that it is good, and that You will finish it.

I did not start this. I have been trying to start things for years and they never held. Something else is going on.

So keep going. Even when I cannot see any difference. Even when I undo a week in one night.

Finish what You started in me.

In Jesus' name, amen.
